extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners, patent agents/applicants, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing novelty (anticipation), inherent/implicit disclosure, and inventive step (obviousness) under the Canadian Patent Act, including the Sanofi four‑step analysis and related tests (e.g., obvious‑to‑try, aggregations, utility). Intended for use during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The information made available must be such that if the person skilled in the art were to write down that information, they would have drafted a clear and unambiguous description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An enabling disclosure makes available the necessary information to practise the invention. The disclosure must permit the skilled person to operate the invention; merely mentioning an idea without enabling details may not anticipate. See also requirements for implicit/inherent disclosure and reverse engineering analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by prior sale or public use (opportunity to access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure may be made if the public has the 'opportunity to access the information that is the invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining whether a publicly available product anticipates, consider the ability of the person skilled in the art to reverse engineer the product 'in accordance with known analytical techniques'. It is enough that reverse engineering would have been possible without inventive effort; it is not necessary to prove that reverse engineering actually occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period for applicant disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering anticipation by prior sale or use, the grace period provided in paragraph 28.2(1)(a) of the Patent Act applies to any making available of the invention by the applicant or by a person who obtained the relevant knowledge directly or indirectly from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grace period (generally one year before filing) excludes the applicant's own disclosures within that period from being treated as prior art for novelty, but such disclosures outside the grace period may be prior art for obviousness assessments as set out in 28.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit or inherent disclosure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An enabling disclosure is considered to disclose everything that would inevitably or necessarily occur or be done by a person practising the invention; inherent and implicit features are included in what is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherent features are properties/characteristics necessarily present (e.g., ductility of a metal); implicit features are things a skilled person would necessarily understand to be part of operation (e.g., means to reduce pressure for 'distillation at reduced pressure'). The mere discovery of properties of a previously disclosed invention does not make it newly patentable unless the discovery leads to a new practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of properties vs new practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere discovery of the properties of a previously disclosed invention does not make that invention newly patentable, but where the discovery leads to a new practical application of the previous invention that new practical application may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discovering a mechanism of action for compound X used to treat disease Y does not make the use novel; but discovering that X could treat disease Z could be patentable if not inherent in the prior disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain implicit/inherent feature findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a conclusion of anticipation requires the presence of an inherent or implicit feature, the examiner must clearly explain the basis for concluding that the feature is implicit or inherent to the prior disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an explanation should set out why the skilled person would inevitably derive the feature; if supported by secondary references, the dates of those references are not important for showing implicit/inherent aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation based on related teachings (single disclosure from multiple sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single prior disclosure can comprise teachings in more than one document only where there is an unambiguous relationship between the two sources such that the primary source directs the reader to use the teachings of the secondary source to understand or complete the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely mentioning another source is insufficient. The first source must direct the reader to the secondary teachings for understanding or operating the invention to treat them together as one disclosure for anticipation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General test for obviousness (inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is obvious (lacks inventive step) if, on the claim date, it would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art in light of their common general knowledge and the state of the art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is assessed claim‑by‑claim. The inquiry allows combining teachings of multiple prior art documents discoverable in a reasonable and diligent search. To be obvious, prior teachings must be sufficient to lead to the claimed invention (or a working embodiment) and it must be obvious to combine those teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as prior art for obviousness (section 28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 28.3 of the Patent Act defines disclosures to be considered for obviousness: public disclosures by the applicant outside the grace period and any third‑party disclosures made before the claim date anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although any public disclosure may be considered in principle, assessments are almost exclusively performed on written disclosures. The grace period excludes applicant disclosures made within one year before filing from being prior art for novelty, but such disclosures before that period are relevant to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness and applicant's prior disclosures (28.3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Information disclosed before the one‑year period immediately preceding the filing date by the applicant or by a person who obtained knowledge from the applicant can be considered when assessing obviousness (subject to the grace period rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision treats applicant disclosures made before the grace period as prior art for obviousness; disclosures within the grace period are excluded. If the claim date is earlier, the relevant period is between the claim date and filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness and third‑party disclosures (28.3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any public disclosure made by a third party before the claim date, anywhere in the world, may be considered as prior art for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third‑party disclosures are not limited by locality; global publications before the claim date are relevant to the obviousness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi four‑step analysis for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A four‑step analysis endorsed by the Supreme Court: (1) identify the notional person skilled in the art and their common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim (or construe it); (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept; (4) asked without knowledge of the invention, would those differences be obvious to the person skilled in the art?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though various tests exist, the Sanofi four‑step analysis frames the inquiry; examiners typically apply it intuitively and should set it out in pre‑final or Final Action reports when there is disagreement with applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (step 1(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the notional 'person skilled in the art' (POSITA); the specification is read and understood from their point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More detail is in section 12.02.02b. The POSITA is presumed to read prior disclosures with a mind willing to understand and desirous of success; they may apply teachings from one source to another and combine teachings. Examiners must use the appropriate knowledge the POSITA would have at the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge (step 1(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Common general knowledge' means knowledge generally known by persons skilled in the relevant art at the relevant time; the relevant time is the claim date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used throughout examination; see section 12.02.02c for further guidance on identifying CGK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the inventive concept (step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventive concept comprises the features of the claim that appear to be inventive over the common general knowledge and/or which the applicant appears to consider inventive; it is a separate exercise from claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposive construction determines essential elements; inventive concept may include a combination of essential elements but need not include all. Identification should be based on reading the specification as a whole from the POSITA perspective in light of CGK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying differences between inventive concept and state of the art (step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the inventive concept to the state of the art to determine whether an equivalent or similar solution was known at the claim date; the state of the art is information available to the POSITA, generally identified by specific prior art documents found in a reasonable and diligent search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no difference, the claim is likely anticipated or obvious. If the prior art is not enabling, the claim may not be anticipated but could still be obvious. Multiple documents may need to be combined to arrive at the inventive concept; differences must be assessed for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the differences constitute an inventive step? (step 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewed without knowledge of the alleged invention, determine whether the differences would have been obvious steps to the POSITA or require inventive ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hindsight. Consider factors including: the climate in the relevant field (attitudes, trends, expectations), any motivation at the time to solve the recognised problem, and the time and effort involved in the invention. Inventive ingenuity may reside in idea, application, or both; beware 'straw man' problems invented to imply inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining teachings from several documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When showing obviousness by combining teachings, the relationship among documents and to the POSITA must be considered; an explanation of why it was obvious to combine the teachings may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasoning for motivation to combine based on the documents themselves, CGK, or trends in the field. Reliance on documents outside the field requires a stronger explanation for applying their teachings to the invention's field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious‑to‑try considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In some fields, an obviousness assessment may ask whether the route to the invention was 'obvious to try', particularly where advances are often obtained by experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include: whether it was self‑evident that what was tried ought to work; whether there were a finite number of predictable solutions; the extent/nature/amount of effort required (routine vs prolonged and arduous); and whether prior art provided motive to find the solution. Examiners recast these as objective questions about what the POSITA would have done on the claim date, avoiding consideration of inventors' subjective experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregations vs unitary result
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere aggregation of elements (each performing its own individual function so removal of one leaves others functioning) is not patentable; combinations that cooperate to produce a unitary and different result may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention is merely a juxtaposition of known parts with no new mode of operation or unitary result, it is a mere aggregation (obvious under section 28.3). Examiners may cite separate prior art documents showing each known part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness and utility (unexpected results and sound prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingenuity of an invention is often related to its utility; unexpected results or new usefulness can support inventiveness, but mere discovery of properties does not confer patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: minor variations (size, shape, proportion) that do the same thing in the same way are not inventive; substituting a superior material expectedly is obvious. New use may be patentable if novel and unobvious. Utility assessment and sound prediction are distinct from obviousness, though interdependent in some cases; sound prediction relies on applicant description, accepted laws, and CGK, while obviousness relies on the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of anticipated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is anticipated by prior art, it will often also be obvious; anticipation typically leads at step 3 to no difference between inventive concept and state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners who identify a lack of novelty need not provide separate analyses for anticipation and obviousness where a single analysis suffices, although both defects may be identified later. Applicants responding to novelty objections should explain why the claimed subject‑matter is unobvious even if obviousness was not explicitly alleged; the Sanofi analysis generally applies.
